title: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part Two: Media Types
subtitle: How an email message says what each piece of it is, and how pieces nest inside one another.
summary: RFC 2046 is the second of the five MIME documents. It defines how the Content-Type header names the kind of data in a message body, using a type and a subtype such as text/plain or image/jpeg. It sets up seven top-level types, five for single kinds of data and two (multipart and message) that hold other messages and parts. This is the structure behind email attachments, HTML-plus-plain-text mail and forwarded messages.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines how the Content-Type header names the kind of data in a message body, using a type and subtype such as text/plain or image/jpeg. It sets up seven top-level types: five for single kinds of data, plus multipart and message, which hold other parts and messages. Email attachments and forwarded messages use this structure.

questions: how does a mime boundary work
what is the default charset for mime text

tldr.problem: Internet mail was built for plain US-ASCII text, with no standard way to say that a body is a picture, a program, several attachments or another whole message.
tldr.mechanism: A Content-Type header names a type and subtype plus parameters. Seven top-level types are defined: text, image, audio, video and application for single kinds of data, and multipart and message for containers. Containers hold other entities; a multipart body separates its parts with boundary lines and parts can nest.
tldr.outcome: Every mail client still labels attachments and HTML mail this way, and the type/subtype names grew into the general media type system also used by HTTP.

today: Almost every email you read uses this document. A message with an attachment is a multipart/mixed body, and a message with both plain text and HTML is multipart/alternative, with the HTML part last. Saving a message as an .eml file stores a message/rfc822 entity, and application/octet-stream is the fallback that web servers and browsers also use for unknown downloads. The type and subtype naming was reused by HTTP's Content-Type header. Several later RFCs update this one, including RFC 2646 (the format parameter), RFC 6657 (charset handling) and RFC 8098 (message disposition notifications).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MIME is a set of five documents that lets Internet mail carry more than plain US-ASCII text. The first, RFC 2045, defines the header fields, including Content-Type. This second document says what goes into that header: a top-level type, a subtype and optional parameters, written as type/subtype; name=value.

The split between type and subtype is the key idea. A program that sees image/xyz knows the body is an image even if it has never heard of format "xyz", so it can decide what is safe to do with it. The RFC gives the example that showing the raw data of an unknown text subtype may be reasonable, but doing the same for an unknown image or audio subtype is not.

Parameters only modify a subtype and do not change the nature of the content. The RFC requires that MIME implementations ignore parameters whose names they do not recognise. New types, subtypes and other values are meant to be added through a registration process run by IANA, described in RFC 2048. This document defines the initial seven top-level types and a few subtypes.

RFC 2046 obsoletes RFC 1521, RFC 1522 and RFC 1590, which were earlier versions of the same MIME work.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME is a set of five documents that let Internet mail carry more than plain US-ASCII text. This second document defines what goes in the Content-Type header: a type, a subtype and optional parameters. A program that sees image/xyz knows it is an image even if it does not know the format.

sections.title: The seven top-level types
sections.content:
Section 3 introduces the initial top-level types. Five are discrete, meaning one kind of data that MIME treats as opaque. Two are composite, meaning they hold other entities that MIME itself processes.

text
Textual information. The subtype plain means text with no formatting commands, shown as-is.
image, audio, video
Data that needs a display or audio device. This document defines image/jpeg, audio/basic and video/mpeg.
application
Everything else: uninterpreted binary data or data meant for a particular program.
multipart and message
Containers. A multipart body holds several parts; a message body holds an encapsulated message or a piece of one.

Sections 4 and 5 define each in turn. The RFC also says that registered subtypes of text, image, audio and video should not hide information of a different type inside them; mixed formats belong in multipart or application.

Section 6 reserves names starting with X- for private, experimental values and discourages inventing new top-level types, since a new subtype of an existing type is nearly always enough. The tree below shows the layout.
sections.plainLanguage: There are seven top-level types. Five are discrete, meaning one kind of data that MIME treats as opaque: text, image, audio, video and application. Two are composite, meaning they contain other entities: multipart holds several parts and message holds a whole message.

sections.title: Text, line breaks and character sets
sections.content:
The text type is for material that is mainly readable text. text/plain is the simplest and most important subtype: no formatting commands, to be displayed as-is. Other text subtypes may add formatting, but a reader without special software should still get the gist.

Two rules matter most. First, the canonical form of any text subtype MUST represent a line break as CRLF, and CR or LF alone may not appear outside a line break. Second, the charset parameter names the character set, for example:

Content-type: text/plain; charset=iso-8859-1

Charset values are not case sensitive. If the parameter is missing, US-ASCII must be assumed. The RFC strongly recommends that new user agents always state a charset explicitly, and says composers should use the "lowest common denominator" set: a body containing only ASCII should be labelled US-ASCII, not ISO-8859-1.

The predefined values are US-ASCII and ISO-8859-X, where X was then 1 through 10. Other names need a formal specification and IANA registration, or a private X- prefix. The name "ASCII" is reserved and must not be used. Headers must stay US-ASCII, with other characters handled by RFC 2047.

Unrecognized text subtypes should be treated as text/plain if the charset is understood. If the charset is also unknown, they should be treated as application/octet-stream.

Later, RFC 6657 updated the charset-default rules for textual types.
sections.plainLanguage: The text type is for material that is mainly readable text. The simplest subtype, text/plain, has no formatting and is shown as is. Line breaks must be written as CRLF. The charset parameter names the character set, for example charset=iso-8859-1.

sections.title: Application and binary data
sections.content:
The application type is for discrete data that does not fit elsewhere, especially data that must be processed by a program before a person can use it. This document defines two subtypes.

application/octet-stream means arbitrary binary data. It has two optional parameters: TYPE, a hint for the human reader, and PADDING, the number of padding bits added to reach a whole number of 8-bit bytes. The older NAME parameter is deprecated in favour of a separate Content-Disposition header, later defined in RFC 2183. The recommended action for a receiver is simply to offer to save the data to a file. Implementations are strongly advised NOT to follow an "interpreter=" style parameter that names a program to run on the body.

application/postscript means a PostScript program, level 1 or level 2. The RFC spends several pages on the security risks of running such programs: a PostScript interpreter can read and write files and change device settings, so receivers are told not to feed bodies to an off-the-shelf interpreter. Printing is described as usually safe because a printer constrains the damage.

The PostScript discussion is the RFC's model for any media type that can cause actions on the recipient's machine.

Because "application" is a catch-all, the subtype is usually named after the program that handles it, though not any program name may be used freely.
sections.plainLanguage: The application type is for data that does not fit elsewhere, especially data a program must process before a person can use it. application/octet-stream means arbitrary binary data. The recommended action for a receiver is to offer to save it to a file.

sections.title: Multipart: many parts in one message
sections.content:
A multipart entity combines several body parts in one body. Its Content-Type must carry a boundary parameter, 1 to 70 characters from a small, gateway-safe set that must not end in whitespace. Each part is introduced by a delimiter line, two hyphens followed by the boundary value, and the last one is followed by a closing line with two more hyphens. The boundary must not appear inside any part.

Each body part looks like a tiny message: optional header fields, a blank line, then the body. No header is required, and only fields beginning with Content- have defined meaning. A part with no Content-Type defaults to text/plain; charset=US-ASCII. Text before the first delimiter (the preamble) and after the closing one (the epilogue) must be ignored, which makes the preamble a handy place for a note to people with non-MIME readers. Multiparts may nest as long as each level uses a different boundary, and a parser must recognise an outer boundary even inside inner content.

All subtypes share this syntax. They differ in meaning:

mixed
Independent parts in a given order. Any unrecognized multipart subtype is to be treated as this.
alternative
The same information in several versions, ordered from plainest to most faithful. Show the last one you can display.
digest
Like mixed, but each part defaults to message/rfc822.
parallel
Order does not matter; parts may be shown at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: A multipart entity combines several body parts in one body. Its Content-Type must include a boundary parameter. Each part starts with a delimiter line of two hyphens followed by the boundary value, and a final line ends the body. Each part looks like a small message with optional headers, a blank line and a body.

sections.title: Message: mail inside mail
sections.content:
The message type is for bodies that are themselves all or part of a message. Three subtypes are defined.

message/rfc822 encapsulates a complete message with RFC 822 syntax. It is how a forwarded or attached email is carried. Only the encodings 7bit, 8bit and binary are allowed on the body, and mail agents may not add, remove or reorder the encapsulated headers. The usual rule that a message must have From, Date and a destination is relaxed: at least one of From, Subject or Date must be present. Despite the name, the content can be a MIME message or even a news article.

message/partial splits a large entity across several messages when a mail system limits size, much as IP fragments packets. It needs three parameters: id (a unique identifier), number (this fragment, counting from 1) and total (required on the last fragment, optional on earlier ones). Fragments must be cut at line boundaries and use 7bit encoding. On reassembly the receiver rebuilds one transparent message whose headers are merged under set rules.

message/external-body carries a reference instead of the data. A mandatory access-type parameter says how to fetch it (FTP, ANON-FTP, TFTP, LOCAL-FILE or MAIL-SERVER are listed), with optional expiration, size and permission parameters. It must include a Content-ID in the encapsulated headers.

Unrecognized message subtypes are treated as application/octet-stream.
sections.plainLanguage: The message type is for bodies that are themselves all or part of a message. message/rfc822 carries a complete message, which is how forwarded or attached email travels. message/partial splits a large message into pieces, and message/external-body points to data kept elsewhere.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
The security section is short and points back to three places in the document. Security issues are discussed in the contexts of application/postscript, message/external-body and the registration rules in RFC 2048.

The RFC asks implementors to pay special attention to any media type that can cause actions on the recipient's machine, and calls the application/postscript discussion a model for how to think about those types.

The external-body type has its own warnings. A message can name a file, an FTP site or a mail server for the receiving agent to contact on the user's behalf, so a hostile sender might try to trick the reader into retrieving material they are not authorized to obtain. The RFC says user agents must describe the action and ask for explicit permission first. Elsewhere the RFC cautions that handing an unknown image, audio or video subtype to a general-purpose viewer inherits the security problems of the most dangerous format that viewer supports, and that a receiver should not search for and run a program named in a Content-Type parameter.

The theme of the whole document: a label tells you how to handle data, not that the data is safe. Treat any type that can run code or contact other systems with caution.
sections.plainLanguage: The security section is short and points to the application/postscript discussion, the message/external-body type and the registration rules. Implementors should take special care with any media type that can cause actions on the recipient's machine. External-body can name a file or server to contact, so a hostile sender might misuse it.

viz.caption: A MULTIPART MESSAGE, FROM THE RFC

data.title: multipart/mixed with preamble and epilogue
data.code:
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-type: multipart/mixed; boundary="simple boundary"

This is the preamble.  It is to be ignored, though it
is a handy place for composition agents to include an
explanatory note to non-MIME conformant readers.

--simple boundary

This is implicitly typed plain US-ASCII text.
It does NOT end with a linebreak.
--simple boundary
Content-type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii

This is explicitly typed plain US-ASCII text.
It DOES end with a linebreak.

--simple boundary--

This is the epilogue.  It is also to be ignored.

data.title: multipart/alternative
data.code:
Content-Type: multipart/alternative; boundary=boundary42

--boundary42
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii

  ... plain text version of message goes here ...

--boundary42
Content-Type: text/enriched

  ... RFC 1896 text/enriched version of same message
      goes here ...

--boundary42
Content-Type: application/x-whatever

  ... fanciest version of same message goes here ...

--boundary42--

viz.caption: MESSAGE/PARTIAL: SENDING ONE ENTITY IN TWO PIECES

messages.note: Split at a line boundary; 7bit encoding only

messages.label: Message 2: message/partial; id="ABC@host.com"; number=2; total=2
messages.note: The last fragment must give total

messages.label: Both fragments delivered, possibly separately
messages.note: Receiver matches on id, orders by number and merges headers; the result is the inner message, e.g. one audio/basic message
